opus-5.5.text:
I think when people look back at AlexNet, sorry, I think you mean AlexNet, they often credit it to a clever new architecture. But honestly, I see it mainly as a story about scaling. The ideas in it, convolutional networks, backpropagation, even ReLU and dropout to some degree, weren't completely new. What was new was that, for the first time, three things came together at a large enough scale: a big labeled dataset in ImageNet, GPU compute that made training a big model practical, and a network with enough capacity to absorb all that data. Once those three were in place, the performance jump was dramatic. That was the moment the field realized that if you scale data, compute, and model together, deep learning really works.

So after AlexNet, the natural question for all of us was: if bigger helps, can we keep going bigger? Especially deeper. VGG pushed depth to around 16 or 19 layers and it worked very well. But when we tried to go further, we hit a wall. Adding more layers actually made things worse, and not just on the test set. The *training* error went up too. That was very strange, because in principle a deeper network should be at least as good as a shallower one. It could just learn identity mappings in the extra layers. So it wasn't overfitting. It was an optimization problem. The network was failing to learn something it should easily be able to represent.

ResNet came out of that observation. The residual connection is a very simple idea: instead of asking each block to learn the full transformation, you let it learn a residual on top of an identity shortcut. If the extra layers aren't useful, they can just learn to output something close to zero, and the signal passes through. With that change, we could train networks with over a hundred layers, even a thousand in experiments, and deeper finally meant better again.

So the way I understand it, AlexNet showed that scaling works, and ResNet removed an obstacle that was stopping us from scaling along the depth dimension. In a sense, ResNet isn't really about a fancy new capability. It's about making optimization easy enough that scale can do its job. And I think that lesson has held up. Residual connections are in basically every large model today, including Transformers. Much of the progress since then follows the same pattern: find the bottleneck that prevents you from scaling, fix it in the simplest way possible, and then let data and compute take you further.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd actually say scaling was the whole point from the beginning, even before we had the word for it. When we were working on the early CNN stuff, the one thing everybody in the group believed in was depth. You add layers, you get better features. That was the intuition, and it kept paying off: VGG went to sixteen, nineteen layers, and it worked. So the natural question was, why stop there?

And then you try to go to thirty, forty, fifty layers, and it just breaks. The training error goes up. Not the test error, the training error. That was the thing that really bothered us, because it means the problem isn't overfitting, it's optimization. A deeper network should be able to represent anything a shallower one can, in theory, by just learning identity mappings in the extra layers. But in practice the solver can't find that solution.

So ResNet, in my mind, wasn't a "new architecture" so much as it was removing the thing that was blocking scaling. The residual connection says, okay, if the extra layers are useless, make it trivial for them to be the identity. Learn the delta instead of the whole function. Once you do that, suddenly 50 layers works, 101 works, 152 works. We even trained a thousand-layer network on CIFAR just to see. And the curve was very clean: more depth, better accuracy, for a long time.

Looking back, I think that was my first real lesson about scaling. The lesson wasn't "bigger is better." Everybody already believed that. The lesson was that when scaling stops working, the first thing you should suspect is that your system has a bottleneck that's hiding the real trend. You're not seeing the limit of scale, you're seeing the limit of your method. Batch norm removed one bottleneck, residuals removed another, and each time the curve just continued.

That mindset stayed with me afterward. In the later work, when we hit saturation again, I didn't assume we'd reached the ceiling. I assumed we were missing something. Sometimes that's the right call and sometimes it isn't, honestly. In vision, for example, I've become more skeptical over the years. You scale the model and the data and at some point the gains really do flatten, and I don't think it's purely an optimization problem anymore. That's a different kind of bottleneck, maybe about what the task itself can teach you. But in 2015 the answer was simple: the depth was there, we just had to let the gradients through.

astra-6.text:
I think scaling is central, but the key question is what allows a model to benefit from greater scale. You can add more layers or more computation, but that doesn’t automatically give you a better network.

That became very concrete in our work on ResNet. We observed that deeper plain networks could have higher training error than shallower ones. So this wasn’t simply an overfitting problem—the deeper network was harder to optimize. In principle, the extra layers could just learn an identity mapping, preserving the shallower network’s solution, but finding that solution through training was difficult.

The residual formulation made that easier: instead of asking a stack of layers to learn the entire mapping, we asked it to learn a correction to its input, with a shortcut carrying the input forward. That helped us train much deeper networks and obtain benefits from the additional depth.

So I see architecture and scaling as closely connected. Scaling gives you an opportunity for greater capability; the architecture helps make that opportunity achievable. I’d just clarify what you mean by XNet before drawing a specific connection to that work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scaling was an important motivation, but the key question was how to make scaling effective. Simply adding layers or increasing computation does not guarantee a better network. You need an architecture that can use that additional capacity and that you can actually optimize.

With ResNet, we focused on a surprising observation: a deeper plain network could have higher training error than a shallower one. That suggested an optimization problem, rather than just overfitting. Residual connections gave the network a way to learn changes to an identity mapping, which made much deeper networks easier to train.

So I would describe the relationship as a feedback loop: scaling exposes limitations in the existing design, and architectural changes make the next stage of scaling useful. I’d want to clarify which work you mean by XNet before drawing a more specific connection to it.
